question.text: Treatment of contralateral hydrocele in neonatal testicular torsion: Is less more?
question.context: Treatment of neonatal testicular torsion has two objectives: salvage of the involved testicle (which is rarely achieved) and preservation of the contralateral gonad. The second goal universally involves contralateral testicular scrotal fixation to prevent the future occurrence of contralateral torsion. However, there is controversy with regards to management of a synchronous contralateral hydrocele. It has been our policy not to address the contralateral hydrocele through an inguinal incision to minimize potential injury to the spermatic cord. Our objective in this study was to determine whether the decision to manage a contralateral hydrocele in cases of neonatal testicular torsion solely through a scrotal approach is safe and effective. We reviewed all cases of neonatal testicular torsion occurring at our institution between the years 1999 and 2006. Age at presentation, physical examination, ultrasonographic and intraoperative findings were recorded. Patients were followed after initial surgical intervention to determine the likelihood of developing a subsequent hydrocele or hernia. Thirty-seven patients were identified as presenting with neonatal torsion. Age of presentation averaged 3.5 days (range 1-14 days). Left-sided pathology was seen more commonly than the right, with a 25:12 distribution. All torsed testicles were nonviable. Twenty-two patients were noted to have a contralateral hydrocele at presentation. All hydroceles were opened through a scrotal approach at the time of contralateral scrotal fixation. No patient underwent an inguinal exploration to examine for a patent process vaginalis. None of the patients who presented with a hydrocele have developed a clinical hydrocele or hernia after an average 7.5 years (range 4.3-11.2) follow-up.

medgemma_4b.clinical_reasoning: The study demonstrates that managing a contralateral hydrocele in neonatal testicular torsion solely through a scrotal approach is safe and effective, as no patients developed a clinical hydrocele or hernia after a significant follow-up period. This suggests that the scrotal approach is sufficient.
medgemma_4b.critical_evidence: No patient who presented with a hydrocele developed a clinical hydrocele or hernia after an average 7.5 years (range 4.3-11.2) follow-up.
medgemma_4b.differential_considered: A differential diagnosis of hydrocele could include other causes of scrotal swelling. However, the study specifically addresses the contralateral hydrocele in the context of neonatal testicular torsion, and the data strongly supports the safety and effectiveness of the scrotal approach in this specific scenario.

rnj1_8b.clinical_reasoning: The study demonstrates that managing contralateral hydroceles through a scrotal approach alone is safe and effective, with no patients developing clinical hydroceles or hernias after 7.5 years of follow-up. This supports the policy of avoiding inguinal incisions to minimize potential injury to the spermatic cord.
rnj1_8b.critical_evidence: No patient developed a clinical hydrocele or hernia after an average 7.5 years follow-up
rnj1_8b.differential_considered: Inguinal hernia was considered but ruled out as none of the patients underwent inguinal exploration and no hernias developed

qwen3_vl_8b.clinical_reasoning: The study demonstrates that managing contralateral hydroceles via a scrotal approach during scrotal fixation in neonatal testicular torsion is safe and effective, with no subsequent hydrocele or hernia development over a long follow-up period. This supports the 'less is more' philosophy by avoiding unnecessary inguinal exploration and potential cord injury.
qwen3_vl_8b.critical_evidence: None of the 22 patients with contralateral hydroceles developed a clinical hydrocele or hernia after an average 7.5 years of follow-up.
qwen3_vl_8b.differential_considered: The differential of contralateral hydrocele as a sign of patent processus vaginalis or impending hernia was considered, but the study explicitly avoided inguinal exploration and found no recurrence, ruling out significant risk from the scrotal approach.

olmo3_7b.clinical_reasoning: The key issue in neonatal testicular torsion is the risk of contralateral torsion if the contralateral testicle is not protected. The case describes that all contralateral hydroceles were managed via scrotal approach without inguinal surgery, and no subsequent hydrocele or hernia developed after a long follow-up. This supports that managing the contralateral hydrocele with scrotal approach is safe and effective, thus the best answer is 'A: yes'.
olmo3_7b.critical_evidence: The absence of hydrocele or hernia after 7.5 years of follow-up in patients whose contralateral hydrocele was managed via scrotal approach, without inguinal exploration, strongly supports the safety and efficacy of this method.
olmo3_7b.differential_considered: Options B and C could be considered if there were complications or recurrence of torsion/hydrocele, but the data clearly show no such complications after scrotal management only.
